newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Siemens 9-month net profit up 3 pct.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Siemens 9-month net profit up 3 pct.

text.p: German industrial group Siemens AG said on Monday net profit in the first nine months of 1996/97 rose three percent to 1.705 billion marks ($953.8 million), thanks to positive currency effects and rising sales of computer communications equipment.

Sales in the period increased 10 percent to 71.2 billion marks, while orders rose 14 percent to 82.8 billion marks. Two percentage points of sales growth and four percentage points of order growth were attributable to favourable currency rates, the company said in a statement.

"Buoyant business in the Americas and Asia-Pacific more than compensated for a light decline in Germany," said Siemens, which previously forecast no increase in profit this year. "Growth was generated exclusively by international business."
Orders in North and South America rose 26 percent to 16.5 billion marks, including a 20 percent rise in U.S. business to 10.7 billion marks.
In Asia, orders climbed 45 percent to 11.5 billion marks, while European orders outside of Germany rose 13 percent to 20.2 billion marks.
Domestic orders fell two percent to 27.2 billion marks, while domestic sales slipped one percent to 24.9 billion marks.
Siemens also said capital spending and investments in the nine months to June 30 rose 28 percent to 6.3 billion marks.

In the nine-month period, Public Communications (ON) sales rose 28 percent to 9.9 billion marks, while Private Communications (PN) sales climbed 12 percent to 7.8 billion marks. Orders at ON rose 26 percent to 13.1 billion marks, while PN orders increased 12 percent 8.2 billion marks.
Computer unit Siemens-Nixdorf Informationssystems AG saw sales in the period rise 11 percent to 10.8 billion marks, while orders increased 13 percent to 11.6 billion marks.
Siemens semiconductor sales rose 20 percent to 4.1 billion marks and ordres increased 19 percent to 4.5 billion marks.

The company's statement gave no guidance on semiconductor profits. A sharp drop in computer chip profit, due to falling memory chip prices, was one of the main reasons Siemens did not expect 1996-97 profit to increase.
Siemens saw difficulty in its KWU power generation business, as sales fell 10 percent to 4.4 billion marks and orders fell three percent to 6.3 billion marks.
